source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2010
setup: I've just been on a once-in-a-lifetime holiday.
punchline: I'll tell you what, never again.
targetAssumption: A dream trip: "once-in-a-lifetime" is how people describe the best holiday they will ever have.
reinterpretation: Once in a lifetime because it was so bad he will never repeat it.
whyItWorks: The phrase is a compliment in the setup and a warning in the punch, and nothing about the facts changes. "I'll tell you what" is a deliberate stall: it sounds like the start of a rave review, so "never again" lands harder.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2010
setup: As a kid I was made to walk the plank.
punchline: We couldn't afford a dog.
targetAssumption: Pirates. "Walk the plank" is a punishment from a story about the high seas.
reinterpretation: He was the plank's pet: a family too poor for a dog "walked" the plank instead, like a dog on a lead.
whyItWorks: Delaney hides a whole second reading behind one verb, "walk". The punch never explains it; the audience builds the picture of a child taking a plank for walkies themselves, which is why the laugh arrives a beat late and big.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2012
setup: I was raised as an only child,
punchline: which really annoyed my sister.
targetAssumption: He has no siblings. That is what "only child" means.
reinterpretation: "Raised as" an only child: his parents treated him as one, and his actual sister noticed.
whyItWorks: The connector is the quiet phrase "raised as", which most listeners skip over. Ending on "sister" is the cleanest possible reveal: one noun contradicts the setup and explains it at the same time.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2016
setup: I've been happily married for four years
punchline: – out of a total of 10.
targetAssumption: Four happy years of a four-year marriage: a sweet anniversary brag.
reinterpretation: He has been married for ten years and only four of them were happy.
whyItWorks: The number stays true and the unit changes: "four years" was never the length of the marriage. "Out of a total of" sounds like an exam score, which makes the confession precise and cold. The joke ends on the number that does the damage.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2022
setup: By my age, my parents had a house and a family, and to be fair to me, so do I –
punchline: but it is the same house and it is the same family.
targetAssumption: She has also become a grown-up homeowner with a family of her own.
reinterpretation: She has the same house and family as her parents had because she still lives with them.
whyItWorks: The setup lets her claim adult success honestly, then the punch repeats "house" and "family" with "same" in front of each. The repetition is the joke: the audience gets the reveal on the first "same" and the second one confirms it.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2009
setup: I'm sure wherever my dad is; he's looking down on us.
punchline: He's not dead, just very condescending.
targetAssumption: His dad has died and is watching over the family from heaven.
reinterpretation: "Looking down on us" as in looking down his nose at them: a snob, alive and well.
whyItWorks: A tender phrase about the dead flips into an insult about the living. "He's not dead" clears the first reading out of the way so that "condescending" can be the last word and the whole joke.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2010
setup: I picked up a hitchhiker.
punchline: You gotta when you hit them.
targetAssumption: He gave a stranger a lift. "Picked up" means offering a ride.
reinterpretation: He literally picked the hitchhiker up off the road after running them over.
whyItWorks: One of the rare great jokes where the punch word is not last: "hit" is the reveal, and "them" trails after it because English needs an object. Emo Philips makes up for it with a casual, matter-of-fact "You gotta", so the horror sounds like everyday road etiquette.

source: stage line, quoted in a 1998 interview and his autobiography Crying with Laughter
setup: They laughed when I said I was going to be a comedian.
punchline: They're not laughing now.
targetAssumption: The classic underdog story: people mocked his dream and he proved them wrong.
reinterpretation: They are not laughing now because he is a comedian, and his act is not funny.
whyItWorks: Monkhouse borrows the shape of a triumphant comeback speech and lets the second sentence mean the opposite. It works because the audience is, at that moment, either laughing or not: the joke is about the room it is told in.

source: stand-up clip, 2017
setup: My name is Rahul
punchline: and I'm not a Gandhi.
targetAssumption: An ordinary introduction: name, then something about himself.
reinterpretation: In India the name Rahul instantly suggests Rahul Gandhi, the Congress politician, so he rules it out like a disclaimer.
whyItWorks: A whole joke built from one association the audience already carries. The punch costs four words because the audience supplies the famous surname themselves; Rahul only has to deny it.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2012
setup: I saw a documentary on how ships are kept together.
punchline: Riveting.
targetAssumption: A dry engineering documentary, which sounds boring.
reinterpretation: "Riveting" means gripping, and ships are held together with rivets.
whyItWorks: The purest pun shape: the setup is deliberately dull so that one word can be both a review and a fact. The punch is a single word, so it is the punch word and it is last.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2014
setup: I've decided to sell my Hoover…
punchline: well, it was just collecting dust.
targetAssumption: He is getting rid of a vacuum cleaner he never uses.
reinterpretation: "Collecting dust" means unused, and collecting dust is a vacuum cleaner's whole job.
whyItWorks: The idiom gives a believable reason to sell anything, which hides the pun. Vine's "well," is the beat where he pretends to justify himself.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2017
setup: I'm not a fan of the new pound coin, but then again,
punchline: I hate all change.
targetAssumption: A grumble about the new coin's design.
reinterpretation: "Change" as in coins, and change as in anything new.
whyItWorks: Topical when it was told (the twelve-sided pound coin had just launched) and still clean today. "But then again" pretends to widen the point into a character flaw, and that is exactly where the pun hides.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2023
setup: I started dating a zookeeper,
punchline: but it turned out he was a cheetah.
targetAssumption: A dating story: something went wrong with the boyfriend.
reinterpretation: He was a cheater, and "cheetah" is a zoo animal.
whyItWorks: The zoo setup loads the animal list in the audience's head, and "turned out he was" is the standard line from a break-up story. The pun word is the last word.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2024
setup: I was going to sail around the globe in the world's smallest ship
punchline: but I bottled it.
targetAssumption: A daring voyage he lost his nerve for.
reinterpretation: A ship in a bottle: "bottled it" means lost his nerve, and tiny ships live in bottles.
whyItWorks: Both meanings are true at once, which is what separates a groan from a laugh. Note "it" after "bottled": the verb needs an object, so the punch word is second to last, and that is fine: "it" is too small to step on the laugh.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2016
setup: My dad has suggested that I register for a donor card.
punchline: He's a man after my own heart.
targetAssumption: A dad giving sensible advice.
reinterpretation: "A man after my own heart" means a kindred spirit, and here he literally wants the heart.
whyItWorks: An idiom that is warm on the surface becomes sinister when read literally next to "donor card". The idiom already ends on "heart", so the punch word lands last for free.

source: her reply to a heckler, told in a 2017 interview about Things They Wouldn't Let Me Say
setup: One time, I joked about periods, and a guy shouted, 'Excuse me. We don't want to know about this'. I replied back, 'Maybe you should know about it because
punchline: a period is how life begins.'
targetAssumption: She is about to give the heckler a biology lesson.
reinterpretation: The thing he finds too gross to hear about is the reason he exists: no periods, no heckler.
whyItWorks: The reply turns his disgust back on him: the thing he does not want to hear about is the reason he exists. It is a putdown without a single insult, which is why it wins the room.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, winner 2011
setup: I needed a password with eight characters
punchline: – so I picked Snow White and the Seven Dwarves.
targetAssumption: A password with eight letters, numbers or symbols.
reinterpretation: "Characters" as in people in a story: Snow White plus seven dwarves is eight characters.
whyItWorks: The connector is a tech word with a second, storybook meaning, and Helm picks the most famous group of eight characters there is. The answer is counted correctly, which is why it feels clever rather than random.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2015
setup: The first time I met my wife, I knew she was a keeper.
punchline: She was wearing massive gloves
targetAssumption: "A keeper" means someone worth holding on to: a romantic first meeting.
reinterpretation: A goalkeeper, identified by her huge gloves.
whyItWorks: The idiom is so familiar that nobody hears the word "keeper" any more. The punch gives one visual clue, gloves, and lets the audience do the rest.

source: stage material
setup: I said, "It's serious, doctor, I've broken my arm in 20 places."
punchline: He said, 'Well stop going to those places.'
targetAssumption: "Twenty places" means twenty fractures in the arm.
reinterpretation: The doctor hears "places" as locations, and gives travel advice.
whyItWorks: A doctor-doctor joke from the master. The literal reading belongs to the doctor, not the patient, so the joke gets a straight man for free. Ends on "places", the connector itself.

source: stand-up, quoted in an NPR retrospective (2007)
setup: I got a king-sized bed. I don't know any kings,
punchline: but if one came over, I guess he'll be comfortable.
targetAssumption: "King-sized" is just a bed size. Nobody thinks about actual kings.
reinterpretation: Hedberg takes the label at its word: the bed is for a visiting king.
whyItWorks: Hedberg's whole method in one line: notice a phrase everyone uses without hearing it, then follow its literal logic calmly to the end. The deadpan "I guess" makes it sound like sensible hosting.

source: Animal Crackers (1930)
setup: One morning, I shot an elephant in my pajamas.
punchline: How he got in my pajamas, I don't know.
targetAssumption: He was wearing pajamas when he shot an elephant.
reinterpretation: "In my pajamas" attaches to the elephant, not to him: the elephant was wearing them.
whyItWorks: The most famous grammatical ambiguity in comedy. The punch word "pajamas" is not last: Groucho adds "I don't know" as a shrug, which costs a little punch but gives his character the last beat. It is a deliberate trade, not a mistake.

source: stage material, quoted in his AP obituary (2004)
setup: When I was born, I was so ugly
punchline: that the doctor slapped my mother
targetAssumption: A newborn gets a slap from the doctor to start breathing.
reinterpretation: The baby was so ugly the doctor punished the person responsible.
whyItWorks: Dangerfield's "no respect" persona in one line: the exaggeration is in who gets slapped, not in how ugly he was. Switching the target of a known ritual is cheaper and funnier than describing the ugliness.

source: stage material, quoted in her NPR obituary (2012)
setup: I was so ugly
punchline: my own Ouija board told me to go to hell.
targetAssumption: A standard "I was so ugly…" self-roast.
reinterpretation: Even the spirit world, which is meant to be on her side, insults her.
whyItWorks: "So X that Y" lives or dies on Y. Diller picks a consequence that is specific (her own Ouija board), impossible and rude, and lets the board deliver the insult in its own voice.

source: stage material, quoted in NPR's Fresh Air memorial (2014)
setup: I'm so boring,
punchline: my answering machine put me on hold.
targetAssumption: A self-deprecating claim about being dull company.
reinterpretation: Even a machine designed to listen to her would rather not.
whyItWorks: A machine with a mind of its own makes the exaggeration picturable. "Hold" is the final word, and the image arrives on it.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2012
setup: My mum's so pessimistic, that if there was an Olympics for pessimism ...
punchline: she wouldn't fancy her chances.
targetAssumption: She would win gold: the "so X that" pattern promises a champion.
reinterpretation: Being the world's best pessimist means expecting to lose, so she would not back herself to win.
whyItWorks: The exaggeration eats itself: winning at pessimism means predicting defeat. The audience expects "she'd win gold" and gets the only answer a true pessimist could give.

source: Cheating, his first stand-up clip (2019)
translation: First I got to college and found weed… I took one puff, and the semester was over.
setup: Pehle toh mein college paunch, mujhe ganja mil gaya… Maine phoonka,
punchline: semester khatam ho gaya.
targetAssumption: A story about trying weed for the first time at college: a funny night.
reinterpretation: One puff and an entire semester vanished.
whyItWorks: Classic exaggeration by consequence. The time jump from one puff to a whole semester does all the work, and Bassi tells it as a flat fact, which is his storytelling style. The punch word comes first in the punchline because Hindi puts the verb last; "khatam ho gaya" (got over) lands the image.

source: Live in Las Vegas
setup: I wasn't afraid of the helicopter, it's just that before you get in one, you have to tell your weight. I looked around and I thought,
punchline: 'Well, if everyone is lying like I'm lying, we're going down.'
targetAssumption: Fear of flying in a helicopter.
reinterpretation: The danger is not the aircraft. It is everyone's vanity about their weight.
whyItWorks: Rudner exaggerates a tiny, true social lie until it becomes a plane crash. The "if everyone is lying like I'm lying" turn is a confession, which keeps the audience on her side.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2018
setup: I think love is like central heating.
punchline: You turn it on before guests arrive and pretend it's like this all the time.
targetAssumption: A cosy comparison: love keeps you warm.
reinterpretation: Love is a performance you switch on for visitors.
whyItWorks: The comparison is the setup; the shared detail is the punch. The detail (heating on for guests) is so true of British homes that the audience recognises the couple instantly.

source: stand-up, quoted on NPR Fresh Air (2007)
setup: a stalker is like
punchline: a private investigator who no one has hired
targetAssumption: A comparison is coming, probably something scary.
reinterpretation: The two jobs involve the same activity; the only difference is that no one asked for one of them.
whyItWorks: Martin finds the one feature that separates two things that look identical, and states it like a dictionary. The punch word is the last, because the whole definition turns on "hired".

source: Homecoming King (Netflix, 2017)
setup: In the middle of the street, my dad's in the middle of the road sweeping glass out of the road
punchline: like he works at like a hate crime barbershop
targetAssumption: A shocking moment after their car windows were smashed in a hate crime.
reinterpretation: His dad calmly sweeps up as if it's the end of an ordinary shift.
whyItWorks: The comparison captures his father's quiet acceptance in one image. It is funny and sad at once: the shop analogy says this happens often enough to be routine.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2009
setup: A spa hotel? It's like a normal hotel,
punchline: only in reception there's a picture of a pebble.
targetAssumption: A spa hotel is a luxury upgrade.
reinterpretation: The only difference is a bit of zen decoration.
whyItWorks: Comparison as a weapon: deflate a fancy thing by finding the smallest real difference. The pebble is perfectly specific, and it is the last word.

source: stand-up, on visiting South Africa
setup: I just came back from South Africa – I was in the motherland! Not my motherland, obviously. Black people's motherland. I'm Indian. We have our own motherland:
punchline: England.
targetAssumption: India: an Indian comic's motherland is India.
reinterpretation: England, the colonial power, which a lot of Indians treat as the place everyone aims to move to.
whyItWorks: A one-word reversal that does history, diaspora and self-mockery at the same time. Peters sets up "our own motherland" so that only one answer seems possible, then gives the opposite.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2017
setup: I've given up asking rhetorical questions.
punchline: What's the point?
targetAssumption: He has dropped a bad habit.
reinterpretation: He explains giving them up with a rhetorical question.
whyItWorks: The joke breaks its own rule in the act of announcing it. Self-contradiction is the shortest kind of reversal.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2022
setup: I spent the whole morning building a time machine,
punchline: so that's four hours of my life that I'm definitely getting back.
targetAssumption: A wasted morning: the phrase "four hours of my life I'll never get back".
reinterpretation: A working time machine means he can get the hours back.
whyItWorks: It flips a well-known complaint ("I'll never get that time back") by inserting the one invention that makes it false. "Definitely" is the smug little word that sells it.

source: stage material
setup: Men like cars, women like clothes.
punchline: I only like cars 'cause they take me to clothes.
targetAssumption: She is about to admit she is the exception who loves cars.
reinterpretation: She does like cars, but only as a way to get to clothes.
whyItWorks: The stereotype is set up, apparently broken, then restored with interest. Ending on "clothes" brings the line back to where it started.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2017
setup: Whenever someone says, 'I don't believe in coincidences.'
punchline: I say, 'Oh my God, me neither!'
targetAssumption: He is about to argue with them.
reinterpretation: He agrees, and calls the agreement itself a coincidence.
whyItWorks: The reply proves the opposite of what it says. "Oh my God" is the act-out that makes it a real moment rather than a paradox on paper.

source: stand-up, quoted in an A.V. Club live review
setup: A lot of people are afraid of heights.
punchline: Not me, I'm afraid of widths
targetAssumption: He is about to confess a phobia, or brag that he has none.
reinterpretation: He swaps the fear to the other dimension, which nobody is afraid of.
whyItWorks: Wright flips one measurement for its neighbour and says it with total seriousness. The made-up phobia is the last word, and his flat delivery sells it as a real medical condition.

source: stage material, quoted by Chortle (2011)
setup: Went to one of those farmers markets the other day –
punchline: bought two farmers…
targetAssumption: A farmers' market is where farmers sell food.
reinterpretation: A market that sells farmers.
whyItWorks: Jones reads the possessive the wrong way round: a fish market sells fish, so a farmers market sells farmers. The punch reuses the connector word, so the audience hears the switch instantly.

source: stand-up, quoted in an A.V. Club interview
setup: Rice is great if you're hungry
punchline: and you want 2,000 of something
targetAssumption: A food recommendation: rice is filling.
reinterpretation: Rice is great only if what you want is a huge count of tiny things.
whyItWorks: Hedberg describes a food by its quantity, not its taste, and the precise number turns a meal into a pile. "Something" is vague on purpose: it shows he is thinking about counting, not eating.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2015
setup: Jesus fed 5,000 people with two fishes and a loaf of bread. That's not a miracle.
punchline: That's tapas
targetAssumption: He is about to explain the miracle away scientifically.
reinterpretation: He judges the miracle by restaurant rules: small plates for a crowd is just tapas.
whyItWorks: Two worlds, scripture and a restaurant menu, meet in one shared detail: tiny portions. The modern word comes last and drags the story into a Spanish bar.

source: short story "The Condemned", The New Yorker (1977)
setup: Cloquet hated reality but realized
punchline: it was still the only place to get a good steak.
targetAssumption: Grand existential despair: a philosopher rejecting reality.
reinterpretation: Reality judged as if it were a restaurant, and it gets a grudging recommendation.
whyItWorks: Allen mixes the vocabulary of philosophy with a restaurant review. The joke is in the drop from "reality" to "steak", the biggest possible gap in seriousness.

source: stand-up clip, 2017
translation: In the middle you have Kejriwal. On odd days you can make jokes about him, on even days you cannot.
setup: Beech mein you have Kejriwal.
punchline: On odd days, you can make jokes about him, on even days you cannot.
targetAssumption: He is listing politicians you can and cannot joke about.
reinterpretation: The rules for joking about Delhi's chief minister follow his own odd-even car-number scheme.
whyItWorks: A mash-up of comedy censorship and traffic policy. The audience needs to know the odd-even rule, and once they do, the logic is perfectly consistent, which is why it is funny.

source: stand-up, on mixing ethnicities
setup: Guy from Cuba, woman from Iceland –
punchline: little "ice cubes".
targetAssumption: A run of mixed-heritage babies, each with a portmanteau name.
reinterpretation: Cuba + Iceland = ice cubes.
whyItWorks: The end of a run: after "pasta-farians" and "hin-jews", the audience knows the pattern, so the final mash-up only needs two country names to land. It is the payoff of a list, which is why it can be so short.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2011
setup: People say, "I'm taking it one day at a time." You know what? So is everybody.
punchline: That's how time works.
targetAssumption: A comforting phrase about coping with something hard.
reinterpretation: It is not a coping strategy; it is just how time passes for everyone.
whyItWorks: Pure attitude: irritation at a phrase everybody says. "You know what?" announces the attitude, and the punch is the most deflating, factual sentence possible.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2023
setup: When women gossip we get called bitchy;
punchline: but when men do it's called a podcast.
targetAssumption: A complaint about a double standard.
reinterpretation: Men's gossip gets microphones and a brand.
whyItWorks: The attitude (this is unfair) is proved with one specific, very modern example. "Podcast" is the last word and the whole argument.

source: Dave Funniest Joke of the Fringe, top 10 2012
setup: You know you're working class when
punchline: your TV is bigger than your bookcase.
targetAssumption: A "you know you're X when" list.
reinterpretation: A class marker spotted in the living room furniture.
whyItWorks: Beckett mocks his own background with affection. The proof is one picturable comparison, and the furniture is the punch.

source: Fool Volume (Netflix, 2025)
setup: If you speak good English, they're like, 'Vir Das is not relatable.'
punchline: NEITHER WAS OPPENHEIMER
targetAssumption: He is going to apologise for his English, or explain himself.
reinterpretation: He compares himself to a hugely successful film about a man no one could relate to.
whyItWorks: Das answers a criticism with a swaggering comparison. The capitals in the review show how he shouts it: attitude is carried in the delivery as much as the words.

source: Rom Com, Edinburgh Fringe 2013
setup: Only about ten per cent of my show is based on me being Asian,
punchline: The other 90 per cent is about my issues with white people.
targetAssumption: He is reassuring the audience that the show is not all about race.
reinterpretation: The other 90% is also about race, just from the other side.
whyItWorks: He sounds like he is playing down the identity material, then doubles it. The deadpan maths is the attitude.

source: White House Correspondents' Dinner (2017)
setup: I would say it is an honor to be here,
punchline: but that would be an alternative fact - it is not.
targetAssumption: The standard polite opening of an awards-dinner speech.
reinterpretation: He borrows the White House's own phrase for a lie to admit the politeness is fake.
whyItWorks: Political attitude in a single sentence. Using the room's own jargon ("alternative fact") turns the joke on the people in charge. "It is not" is the plain, blunt last beat.

source: This Is a Book (2011)
setup: The bird, the bee,
punchline: the running child are all the same to the sliding glass door.
targetAssumption: A list of small flying creatures: nature, birds and bees.
reinterpretation: The third item is a child, and what they share is crashing into a glass door.
whyItWorks: Two items set a pattern (things that fly), the third breaks it, and the punch reveals the real category. Martin pushes the reveal to the very last word, "door".
